about.title: Grand Terrace Product Liability Claims
about.longDescription: A defective product doesn't announce itself before it fails — a faulty vehicle part gives out along I-215, a household appliance malfunctions in a Grand Terrace kitchen, or a piece of equipment breaks in a way it never should have. Under California law, injured residents generally don't need to prove a manufacturer was negligent; they need to show the product itself was defective — in its design, its manufacturing, or its warnings — and that the defect caused harm. That's what makes these strict liability claims different from typical negligence cases. Grand Terrace sits between busier San Bernardino County corridors, and residents here encounter the same range of consumer products, vehicles, tools, and machinery as anywhere else, meaning the same risks apply. If a defective product has hurt you or someone you love, keeping the item itself — rather than repairing, discarding, or returning it — matters a great deal. LawProactive offers a free, no-obligation way to connect with an attorney experienced in these claims, who works on contingency, so there's no upfront cost to find out where you stand.

whyChoose.title: Why Strict Liability Changes the Conversation

items.title: No Need to Prove Negligence
items.desc: Because California allows strict liability claims for defective products, the focus stays on whether the product itself was flawed — not on digging through a manufacturer's internal decisions.

items.title: Multiple Parties May Share Responsibility
items.desc: Manufacturers, distributors, and retailers can all potentially be held liable, which often gives an injured person more than one avenue to pursue.

items.title: Preserving the Product Matters Early On
items.desc: Since design, manufacturing, or warning defects must be shown, keeping the product intact and unaltered can be critical evidence an attorney can evaluate.

items.question: Do I have to prove the manufacturer was careless?
items.answer: Not necessarily. Under California's strict liability rules, you generally only need to show the product was defective and that the defect caused your injury. This is different from many other injury claims where negligence must be established.

items.question: What should I do with the product that hurt me?
items.answer: Try to preserve it exactly as it was at the time of the injury, without cleaning, repairing, or discarding it. The product itself is often the most important piece of evidence in these cases, so an attorney will want to examine it.
